# 🧱 mBlock beginner examples: Controller PS4/PS5

[🔙 Back to the Controller PS4/PS5 product page](/en/sensors/ps4/index.md)

This page is for people who have **never written a program**: read the Controller PS4/PS5 on an **mBot** with mBlock 5 blocks. The 5 examples start with "turn the number into a sound" and work up to a robot that drives itself. Every example has a block picture, a downloadable project file and an Arduino sketch that does the same thing.

| Software | Who it suits | How to open the example file |
|---|---|---|
| 🟧 **mBlock 5 desktop** (blocks, Upload mode) + **MBC Pro Sensors extension v2** | Schools, first time with an mBot | Download the `.mblock` → open mBlock 5 → "File → Open from your computer" → switch to "Upload" at the bottom right → "Upload" |
| 🔧 **Arduino IDE** (text code) | People who want to see what is behind the blocks, or write their own code | Download the `.ino` → install the Makeblock and MBC_Sensors libraries (see [Makeblock extension](/en/makeblock.md)) → board Arduino Uno → upload |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> - The sensor must be the **Makeblock edition with the 2026-10 protocol v2 firmware**, connected through the **mBot socket board** to an RJ25 port; use extension **v2.0.0** (old firmware goes with the old v1 extension; they cannot be mixed).
> - The board is the **mBot (mCore)**. mBot Ranger, Orion and MegaPi work too: swap "when mBot starts up" for that board's hat block and use a port that board allows (see [supported boards and ports](/en/makeblock.md)); the mBot2 (CyberPi) has no RJ25 port and is not supported.
> - mBlock 5 is shown here with its English block text; your copy may show the same blocks in another language.

## Before you start

<figure class="ref-fig"><img src="/images/figures/ps4/wiring-mbot.svg" alt="Controller PS4/PS5 × mBot wiring" loading="lazy"></figure>

Sensor → mBot socket board → RJ25 port on the board (S1 = host TX, S2 = host RX, UART 38400).

1. **Install the extension**: get the **MBC Pro Sensors v2.0.0** `.mext` from [Makeblock extension](/en/makeblock.md) and drop it into the mBlock 5 window; add **mBot** under "Devices" (bottom left) and switch to "Upload" (bottom right).
2. **Wiring**: Controller → mBot socket board → mBot **port 4** (every example on this page uses this port; to use another, change the port number on the blocks).
3. **Let it boot first**: every example starts with "wait 1 seconds" so the sensor can boot; reading too early gives -32768 (nothing received yet).
4. **Pair the gamepad (once)**: plug in the receiver and power the mBot on, **without holding the button on the receiver**. The first time it opens pairing for 30 s automatically (green LED blinking fast); to pair a different gamepad press the receiver button (Reset) to open another 30 s. Within those 30 s hold **SHARE + PS** on a PS4 gamepad, or **Create + PS** on a PS5 gamepad, until the light bar blinks fast. The receiver remembers that gamepad; afterwards press **PS** and it reconnects.
5. Receiver LED: blinking fast = waiting to pair, steady on = not connected (press PS), off = connected. **How do you know?** Run example 5: green LED when connected.

## Blocks used on this page

Each reporter block is one "value id" of the sensor's value table (the same ids as the Arduino I2C registers); the full block list is in [Makeblock extension](/en/makeblock.md).

| Block | Returns | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Controller port [4] stick [left stick x / left stick y / right stick x / right stick y] | -100~+100 | 10 LX, 11 LY, 12 RX, 13 RY: −100 to +100, 0 = centre, right/up positive; 0 when not connected |
| Controller port [4] [Ⅹ / ● / ▲ / ■ / up / down / left / right / L1 / R1 / L2 / R2 / L3 / R3 / SELECT / START] pressed? | true / false | one button split out of 16 buttons 01 |
| Controller port [4] gamepad connected? | true / false | 1 = gamepad connected and data seen within 300 ms, 0 = not connected (buttons 0, sticks centred while disconnected) |

**Examples on this page**

1. [The stick changes the pitch](#example-1-the-stick-changes-the-pitch)
2. [Buttons light the LED](#example-2-buttons-light-the-led)
3. [The left stick drives one wheel](#example-3-the-left-stick-drives-one-wheel)
4. [D-pad driving](#example-4-d-pad-driving)
5. [Tank drive + stop when disconnected](#example-5-tank-drive-stop-when-disconnected)

> [!NOTE]
> The `.mblock` files are generated in the mBlock 5 save format and **have not yet been opened in mBlock 5 for verification** (pending the extension v2 release). If one will not open or shows blank blocks, check that extension v2 is loaded and the device is mBot, or rebuild it from the block picture below (under 5 minutes); you can also [tell us on LINE](https://line.me/R/ti/p/@692vcvuk).

## Example 1: The stick changes the pitch

**What this example does**: The mBot has no screen, so this example turns "left stick y" (−100 to +100, 0 when released) into a pitch: push up for a higher note, pull down for a lower one. Learn to "read the number" first.

**What you need**
- mBot (mCore board) + mBlock 5 desktop
- Controller PS4/PS5 Bluetooth receiver (Makeblock edition) + gamepad + mBot socket board

**Wiring**: Bluetooth receiver → mBot socket board → mBot **port 4**. Pair the gamepad once as in "Before you start"; afterwards press the PS button and it reconnects by itself.

**Download**

| mBlock 5 project | Equivalent Arduino sketch |
|---|---|
| [ex01_stick_tone.mblock](/examples/ps4/mblock/ex01_stick_tone.mblock) | [ex01_stick_tone.ino](/examples/ps4/mblock/ex01_stick_tone/ex01_stick_tone.ino) |

<details open>
<summary>🧱 mBlock blocks (just rebuild them like this)</summary>

<pre class="blocks">when mBot starts up :: events hat
wait (1) seconds
forever
  play tone ((440) + ((Controller port [4 v] stick [left stick y v] :: #2B6CD8) * (3))) Hz for (0.1) seconds :: sound
end</pre>

</details>

<details>
<summary>🔧 Equivalent Arduino sketch (mBot)</summary>

```cpp
// Controller PS4/PS5 × mBlock 5  Example 1: The stick changes the pitch  (equivalent Arduino sketch for mBot)
// Wiring: Bluetooth receiver → mBot socket board → mBot port 4. Pair the gamepad once as in "Before you start"; afterwards press the PS button and it reconnects by itself.
// Does exactly what the mBlock block example does, for people who want to see "what is behind the blocks" or use the Arduino IDE.
// Libraries needed:
//   1. Makeblock (Arduino IDE Library Manager, search "Makeblock", or the copy inside the mBlock 5 install folder)
//   2. MBC_Sensors v2: the four files in src/ of the extension .mext (MBC_Sensors.h/.cpp, mbc_proto.h, mbc_ids.h),
//      put them in Documents/Arduino/libraries/MBC_Sensors/ and #include <MBC_Sensors.h> (https://mbc-pro-sensors.github.io/en/makeblock.html)
// Board: Arduino Uno (the mBot mCore is an Uno). After uploading, unplug USB and run on battery.

#include <MeMCore.h>            // mBot (mCore): motors, LED, buzzer
#include <SoftwareSerial.h>
#include <MBC_Sensors.h>        // MBC sensors v2 (the same library the mBlock extension uses)

MBCPort mbc_port4(4);           // sensor on mBot port 4
MeDCMotor motorL(9);           // left wheel (M1)
MeDCMotor motorR(10);          // right wheel (M2)
MeRGBLed rgbled(7, 2);         // on-board RGB LED (2 pixels)
MeBuzzer buzzer;               // on-board buzzer

// left / right wheel power -100~100 (positive = forward): the mBot left wheel is mounted mirrored, so M1 gets the negative value; % becomes PWM 0~255
void wheels(int l, int r) {
  l = constrain(l, -100, 100); r = constrain(r, -100, 100);
  motorL.run(-l * 255 / 100);
  motorR.run(r * 255 / 100);
}

void setup() {   // everything runs inside setup(), just like the program mBlock generates
  mbc_port4.begin();
  delay(1000);   // Wait 1 s for the receiver to boot
  while (1) {   // Repeat forever
    // Pitch = 440 + left stick y × 3 Hz, for 0.1 s
    buzzer.tone((440 + (mbcReadN(mbc_port4, 0x10, 2, 4) * 3)), 100);
  }
}

void loop() {}   // nothing here: the blocks above never return
```

</details>

**Step by step**
1. Wait 1 s for the receiver to boot
2. Repeat forever
   - Pitch = 440 + left stick y × 3 Hz, for 0.1 s

**What you should see**: Stick released: 440 Hz (A). Pushed fully up: 740 Hz; pulled fully down: 140 Hz. With no gamepad connected the stick also reads 0, so 440 Hz too.

**FAQ**
- **No sound?** → The buzzer is on the board and is not loud; listen closely, or change 0.1 s to 0.3 s.
- **Want the right stick or left/right?** → Change the dropdown to "right stick y" or "left stick x".
- **Buttons and sticks do nothing?** → The gamepad is not connected: run example 5 and check the LED. Red = not connected; power-cycle the gamepad (PS4: press PS), or power the mBot on before plugging in the receiver.
- **Nothing happens, or the value stays at -32768?** → Wrong port (every example on this page uses port 4), socket board not seated, or the sensor is not the Makeblock edition. Check with the "MBC common → connected?" block first; "protocol version" must read 2 for the new firmware (old firmware needs extension v1).
- **Upload fails, or the blocks are blank?** → Make sure the switch at the bottom right is in "Upload" mode, extension v2 has been dropped into mBlock, and the USB cable goes to the mBot board.

## Example 2: Buttons light the LED

**What this example does**: With "if… then… else…" and the "pressed?" block: ▲ green, ● red, Ⅹ blue, ■ pink (the colours of the symbols on the gamepad); nothing pressed → LED off.

**What you need**
- mBot (mCore board) + mBlock 5 desktop
- Controller PS4/PS5 Bluetooth receiver (Makeblock edition) + gamepad + mBot socket board

**Wiring**: Bluetooth receiver → mBot socket board → mBot **port 4**. Pair the gamepad once as in "Before you start"; afterwards press the PS button and it reconnects by itself.

**Download**

| mBlock 5 project | Equivalent Arduino sketch |
|---|---|
| [ex02_button_led.mblock](/examples/ps4/mblock/ex02_button_led.mblock) | [ex02_button_led.ino](/examples/ps4/mblock/ex02_button_led/ex02_button_led.ino) |

<details open>
<summary>🧱 mBlock blocks (just rebuild them like this)</summary>

<pre class="blocks">when mBot starts up :: events hat
wait (1) seconds
forever
  if &lt;Controller port [4 v] [▲ v] pressed? :: #2B6CD8&gt; then
    LED [all v] colour red (0) green (255) blue (0) :: looks
  else
    if &lt;Controller port [4 v] [● v] pressed? :: #2B6CD8&gt; then
      LED [all v] colour red (255) green (0) blue (0) :: looks
    else
      if &lt;Controller port [4 v] [Ⅹ v] pressed? :: #2B6CD8&gt; then
        LED [all v] colour red (0) green (0) blue (255) :: looks
      else
        if &lt;Controller port [4 v] [■ v] pressed? :: #2B6CD8&gt; then
          LED [all v] colour red (255) green (0) blue (255) :: looks
        else
          LED [all v] colour red (0) green (0) blue (0) :: looks
        end
      end
    end
  end
end</pre>

</details>

<details>
<summary>🔧 Equivalent Arduino sketch (mBot)</summary>

```cpp
// Controller PS4/PS5 × mBlock 5  Example 2: Buttons light the LED  (equivalent Arduino sketch for mBot)
// Wiring: Bluetooth receiver → mBot socket board → mBot port 4. Pair the gamepad once as in "Before you start"; afterwards press the PS button and it reconnects by itself.
// Does exactly what the mBlock block example does, for people who want to see "what is behind the blocks" or use the Arduino IDE.
// Libraries needed:
//   1. Makeblock (Arduino IDE Library Manager, search "Makeblock", or the copy inside the mBlock 5 install folder)
//   2. MBC_Sensors v2: the four files in src/ of the extension .mext (MBC_Sensors.h/.cpp, mbc_proto.h, mbc_ids.h),
//      put them in Documents/Arduino/libraries/MBC_Sensors/ and #include <MBC_Sensors.h> (https://mbc-pro-sensors.github.io/en/makeblock.html)
// Board: Arduino Uno (the mBot mCore is an Uno). After uploading, unplug USB and run on battery.

#include <MeMCore.h>            // mBot (mCore): motors, LED, buzzer
#include <SoftwareSerial.h>
#include <MBC_Sensors.h>        // MBC sensors v2 (the same library the mBlock extension uses)

MBCPort mbc_port4(4);           // sensor on mBot port 4
MeDCMotor motorL(9);           // left wheel (M1)
MeDCMotor motorR(10);          // right wheel (M2)
MeRGBLed rgbled(7, 2);         // on-board RGB LED (2 pixels)
MeBuzzer buzzer;               // on-board buzzer

// left / right wheel power -100~100 (positive = forward): the mBot left wheel is mounted mirrored, so M1 gets the negative value; % becomes PWM 0~255
void wheels(int l, int r) {
  l = constrain(l, -100, 100); r = constrain(r, -100, 100);
  motorL.run(-l * 255 / 100);
  motorR.run(r * 255 / 100);
}

void setup() {   // everything runs inside setup(), just like the program mBlock generates
  mbc_port4.begin();
  delay(1000);   // Wait 1 s for the receiver to boot
  while (1) {   // Repeat forever
    if (mbcPadPressed(mbc_port4, 12)) {   // If ▲ is pressed
      rgbled.setColor(0, 0, 255, 0); rgbled.show();   // ▲: green
    } else {
      if (mbcPadPressed(mbc_port4, 13)) {   // Otherwise, if ● is pressed
        rgbled.setColor(0, 255, 0, 0); rgbled.show();   // ●: red
      } else {
        if (mbcPadPressed(mbc_port4, 14)) {   // Otherwise, if Ⅹ is pressed
          rgbled.setColor(0, 0, 0, 255); rgbled.show();   // Ⅹ: blue
        } else {
          if (mbcPadPressed(mbc_port4, 15)) {   // Otherwise, if ■ is pressed
            rgbled.setColor(0, 255, 0, 255); rgbled.show();   // ■: pink
          } else {
            rgbled.setColor(0, 0, 0, 0); rgbled.show();   // Nothing pressed: LED off
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

void loop() {}   // nothing here: the blocks above never return
```

</details>

**Step by step**
1. Wait 1 s for the receiver to boot
2. Repeat forever
   - If ▲ is pressed
      - ▲: green
      - otherwise:
         - Otherwise, if ● is pressed
            - ●: red
            - otherwise:
               - Otherwise, if Ⅹ is pressed
                  - Ⅹ: blue
                  - otherwise:
                     - Otherwise, if ■ is pressed
                        - ■: pink
                        - otherwise:
                           - Nothing pressed: LED off

**What you should see**: Hold ▲: green; release: off. ▲ and ● together: green (the first "if" that is true wins).

**FAQ**
- **Want the D-pad or L1 / R1?** → The "pressed?" dropdown lists all 16 buttons.
- **Buttons and sticks do nothing?** → The gamepad is not connected: run example 5 and check the LED. Red = not connected; power-cycle the gamepad (PS4: press PS), or power the mBot on before plugging in the receiver.
- **Nothing happens, or the value stays at -32768?** → Wrong port (every example on this page uses port 4), socket board not seated, or the sensor is not the Makeblock edition. Check with the "MBC common → connected?" block first; "protocol version" must read 2 for the new firmware (old firmware needs extension v1).
- **Upload fails, or the blocks are blank?** → Make sure the switch at the bottom right is in "Upload" mode, extension v2 has been dropped into mBlock, and the USB cable goes to the mBot board.

## Example 3: The left stick drives one wheel

**What this example does**: The stick value −100 to +100 is exactly the motor power range, so use "left stick y" directly as the left wheel power: push more = faster, pull down = reverse, release = stop. Prop the robot up to watch.

**What you need**
- mBot (mCore board) + mBlock 5 desktop
- mBot two-wheel robot (left wheel on M1, right wheel on M2, as shipped)
- Controller PS4/PS5 Bluetooth receiver (Makeblock edition) + gamepad + mBot socket board

**Wiring**: Bluetooth receiver → mBot socket board → mBot **port 4**. Pair the gamepad once as in "Before you start"; afterwards press the PS button and it reconnects by itself.

**Download**

| mBlock 5 project | Equivalent Arduino sketch |
|---|---|
| [ex03_stick_one_wheel.mblock](/examples/ps4/mblock/ex03_stick_one_wheel.mblock) | [ex03_stick_one_wheel.ino](/examples/ps4/mblock/ex03_stick_one_wheel/ex03_stick_one_wheel.ino) |

<details open>
<summary>🧱 mBlock blocks (just rebuild them like this)</summary>

<pre class="blocks">when mBot starts up :: events hat
wait (1) seconds
forever
  left wheel power (Controller port [4 v] stick [left stick y v] :: #2B6CD8) %, right wheel power (0) % :: motion
end</pre>

</details>

<details>
<summary>🔧 Equivalent Arduino sketch (mBot)</summary>

```cpp
// Controller PS4/PS5 × mBlock 5  Example 3: The left stick drives one wheel  (equivalent Arduino sketch for mBot)
// Wiring: Bluetooth receiver → mBot socket board → mBot port 4. Pair the gamepad once as in "Before you start"; afterwards press the PS button and it reconnects by itself.
// Does exactly what the mBlock block example does, for people who want to see "what is behind the blocks" or use the Arduino IDE.
// Libraries needed:
//   1. Makeblock (Arduino IDE Library Manager, search "Makeblock", or the copy inside the mBlock 5 install folder)
//   2. MBC_Sensors v2: the four files in src/ of the extension .mext (MBC_Sensors.h/.cpp, mbc_proto.h, mbc_ids.h),
//      put them in Documents/Arduino/libraries/MBC_Sensors/ and #include <MBC_Sensors.h> (https://mbc-pro-sensors.github.io/en/makeblock.html)
// Board: Arduino Uno (the mBot mCore is an Uno). After uploading, unplug USB and run on battery.

#include <MeMCore.h>            // mBot (mCore): motors, LED, buzzer
#include <SoftwareSerial.h>
#include <MBC_Sensors.h>        // MBC sensors v2 (the same library the mBlock extension uses)

MBCPort mbc_port4(4);           // sensor on mBot port 4
MeDCMotor motorL(9);           // left wheel (M1)
MeDCMotor motorR(10);          // right wheel (M2)
MeRGBLed rgbled(7, 2);         // on-board RGB LED (2 pixels)
MeBuzzer buzzer;               // on-board buzzer

// left / right wheel power -100~100 (positive = forward): the mBot left wheel is mounted mirrored, so M1 gets the negative value; % becomes PWM 0~255
void wheels(int l, int r) {
  l = constrain(l, -100, 100); r = constrain(r, -100, 100);
  motorL.run(-l * 255 / 100);
  motorR.run(r * 255 / 100);
}

void setup() {   // everything runs inside setup(), just like the program mBlock generates
  mbc_port4.begin();
  delay(1000);   // Wait 1 s for the receiver to boot
  while (1) {   // Repeat forever
    wheels(mbcReadN(mbc_port4, 0x10, 2, 4), 0);   // Left wheel power = left stick y (−100 to +100), right wheel 0
  }
}

void loop() {}   // nothing here: the blocks above never return
```

</details>

**Step by step**
1. Wait 1 s for the receiver to boot
2. Repeat forever
   - Left wheel power = left stick y (−100 to +100), right wheel 0

**What you should see**: Push the left stick up: the left wheel turns forward, faster the more you push; pull down: reverse; release: stop.

**FAQ**
- **The robot turns the wrong way and gets worse?** → Swap the "+" and "−" (or swap the left and right wheel powers). The mBot ships with the left wheel on M1 and the right on M2; check your own wiring.
- **Buttons and sticks do nothing?** → The gamepad is not connected: run example 5 and check the LED. Red = not connected; power-cycle the gamepad (PS4: press PS), or power the mBot on before plugging in the receiver.
- **Nothing happens, or the value stays at -32768?** → Wrong port (every example on this page uses port 4), socket board not seated, or the sensor is not the Makeblock edition. Check with the "MBC common → connected?" block first; "protocol version" must read 2 for the new firmware (old firmware needs extension v1).
- **Upload fails, or the blocks are blank?** → Make sure the switch at the bottom right is in "Upload" mode, extension v2 has been dropped into mBlock, and the USB cable goes to the mBot board.

## Example 4: D-pad driving

**What this example does**: Hold a D-pad button and the robot moves that way; release and it stops: up = forward, down = backward, left = spin left, right = spin right.

**What you need**
- mBot (mCore board) + mBlock 5 desktop
- mBot two-wheel robot (left wheel on M1, right wheel on M2, as shipped)
- Controller PS4/PS5 Bluetooth receiver (Makeblock edition) + gamepad + mBot socket board

**Wiring**: Bluetooth receiver → mBot socket board → mBot **port 4**. Pair the gamepad once as in "Before you start"; afterwards press the PS button and it reconnects by itself.

**Download**

| mBlock 5 project | Equivalent Arduino sketch |
|---|---|
| [ex04_dpad_drive.mblock](/examples/ps4/mblock/ex04_dpad_drive.mblock) | [ex04_dpad_drive.ino](/examples/ps4/mblock/ex04_dpad_drive/ex04_dpad_drive.ino) |

<details open>
<summary>🧱 mBlock blocks (just rebuild them like this)</summary>

<pre class="blocks">when mBot starts up :: events hat
wait (1) seconds
forever
  if &lt;Controller port [4 v] [up v] pressed? :: #2B6CD8&gt; then
    left wheel power (50) %, right wheel power (50) % :: motion
  else
    if &lt;Controller port [4 v] [down v] pressed? :: #2B6CD8&gt; then
      left wheel power (-50) %, right wheel power (-50) % :: motion
    else
      if &lt;Controller port [4 v] [left v] pressed? :: #2B6CD8&gt; then
        left wheel power (-30) %, right wheel power (30) % :: motion
      else
        if &lt;Controller port [4 v] [right v] pressed? :: #2B6CD8&gt; then
          left wheel power (30) %, right wheel power (-30) % :: motion
        else
          stop moving :: motion
        end
      end
    end
  end
end</pre>

</details>

<details>
<summary>🔧 Equivalent Arduino sketch (mBot)</summary>

```cpp
// Controller PS4/PS5 × mBlock 5  Example 4: D-pad driving  (equivalent Arduino sketch for mBot)
// Wiring: Bluetooth receiver → mBot socket board → mBot port 4. Pair the gamepad once as in "Before you start"; afterwards press the PS button and it reconnects by itself.
// Does exactly what the mBlock block example does, for people who want to see "what is behind the blocks" or use the Arduino IDE.
// Libraries needed:
//   1. Makeblock (Arduino IDE Library Manager, search "Makeblock", or the copy inside the mBlock 5 install folder)
//   2. MBC_Sensors v2: the four files in src/ of the extension .mext (MBC_Sensors.h/.cpp, mbc_proto.h, mbc_ids.h),
//      put them in Documents/Arduino/libraries/MBC_Sensors/ and #include <MBC_Sensors.h> (https://mbc-pro-sensors.github.io/en/makeblock.html)
// Board: Arduino Uno (the mBot mCore is an Uno). After uploading, unplug USB and run on battery.

#include <MeMCore.h>            // mBot (mCore): motors, LED, buzzer
#include <SoftwareSerial.h>
#include <MBC_Sensors.h>        // MBC sensors v2 (the same library the mBlock extension uses)

MBCPort mbc_port4(4);           // sensor on mBot port 4
MeDCMotor motorL(9);           // left wheel (M1)
MeDCMotor motorR(10);          // right wheel (M2)
MeRGBLed rgbled(7, 2);         // on-board RGB LED (2 pixels)
MeBuzzer buzzer;               // on-board buzzer

// left / right wheel power -100~100 (positive = forward): the mBot left wheel is mounted mirrored, so M1 gets the negative value; % becomes PWM 0~255
void wheels(int l, int r) {
  l = constrain(l, -100, 100); r = constrain(r, -100, 100);
  motorL.run(-l * 255 / 100);
  motorR.run(r * 255 / 100);
}

void setup() {   // everything runs inside setup(), just like the program mBlock generates
  mbc_port4.begin();
  delay(1000);   // Wait 1 s for the receiver to boot
  while (1) {   // Repeat forever
    if (mbcPadPressed(mbc_port4, 4)) {   // If up is pressed
      wheels(50, 50);   // Up: forward
    } else {
      if (mbcPadPressed(mbc_port4, 6)) {   // Otherwise, if down is pressed
        wheels(-50, -50);   // Down: backward
      } else {
        if (mbcPadPressed(mbc_port4, 7)) {   // Otherwise, if left is pressed
          wheels(-30, 30);   // Left: spin left (left wheel back, right wheel forward)
        } else {
          if (mbcPadPressed(mbc_port4, 5)) {   // Otherwise, if right is pressed
            wheels(30, -30);   // Right: spin right
          } else {
            wheels(0, 0);   // Nothing pressed: stop
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

void loop() {}   // nothing here: the blocks above never return
```

</details>

**Step by step**
1. Wait 1 s for the receiver to boot
2. Repeat forever
   - If up is pressed
      - Up: forward
      - otherwise:
         - Otherwise, if down is pressed
            - Down: backward
            - otherwise:
               - Otherwise, if left is pressed
                  - Left: spin left (left wheel back, right wheel forward)
                  - otherwise:
                     - Otherwise, if right is pressed
                        - Right: spin right
                        - otherwise:
                           - Nothing pressed: stop

**What you should see**: Hold up and the robot drives forward; release and it stops.

**FAQ**
- **The robot turns the wrong way and gets worse?** → Swap the "+" and "−" (or swap the left and right wheel powers). The mBot ships with the left wheel on M1 and the right on M2; check your own wiring.
- **Gamepad battery dies or goes out of range?** → If the receiver hears nothing for 0.3 s it releases every button and centres the sticks, so the robot stops by itself.
- **Buttons and sticks do nothing?** → The gamepad is not connected: run example 5 and check the LED. Red = not connected; power-cycle the gamepad (PS4: press PS), or power the mBot on before plugging in the receiver.
- **Nothing happens, or the value stays at -32768?** → Wrong port (every example on this page uses port 4), socket board not seated, or the sensor is not the Makeblock edition. Check with the "MBC common → connected?" block first; "protocol version" must read 2 for the new firmware (old firmware needs extension v1).
- **Upload fails, or the blocks are blank?** → Make sure the switch at the bottom right is in "Upload" mode, extension v2 has been dropped into mBlock, and the USB cable goes to the mBot board.

---

## Example 5: Tank drive + stop when disconnected

**What this example does**: Drive like a tank: the left stick drives the left wheel, the right stick the right wheel, value × 0.7 as power (70 max). "gamepad connected?" guards it: connected → green LED and drive; not connected → stop with a red LED.

**What you need**
- mBot (mCore board) + mBlock 5 desktop
- mBot two-wheel robot (left wheel on M1, right wheel on M2, as shipped)
- Controller PS4/PS5 Bluetooth receiver (Makeblock edition) + gamepad + mBot socket board

**Wiring**: Bluetooth receiver → mBot socket board → mBot **port 4**. Pair the gamepad once as in "Before you start"; afterwards press the PS button and it reconnects by itself.

**Download**

| mBlock 5 project | Equivalent Arduino sketch |
|---|---|
| [ex05_tank.mblock](/examples/ps4/mblock/ex05_tank.mblock) | [ex05_tank.ino](/examples/ps4/mblock/ex05_tank/ex05_tank.ino) |

<details open>
<summary>🧱 mBlock blocks (just rebuild them like this)</summary>

<pre class="blocks">when mBot starts up :: events hat
wait (1) seconds
forever
  if &lt;Controller port [4 v] gamepad connected? :: #2B6CD8&gt; then
    LED [all v] colour red (0) green (255) blue (0) :: looks
    left wheel power ((Controller port [4 v] stick [left stick y v] :: #2B6CD8) * (0.7)) %, right wheel power ((Controller port [4 v] stick [right stick y v] :: #2B6CD8) * (0.7)) % :: motion
  else
    LED [all v] colour red (255) green (0) blue (0) :: looks
    stop moving :: motion
  end
end</pre>

</details>

<details>
<summary>🔧 Equivalent Arduino sketch (mBot)</summary>

```cpp
// Controller PS4/PS5 × mBlock 5  Example 5: Tank drive + stop when disconnected  (equivalent Arduino sketch for mBot)
// Wiring: Bluetooth receiver → mBot socket board → mBot port 4. Pair the gamepad once as in "Before you start"; afterwards press the PS button and it reconnects by itself.
// Does exactly what the mBlock block example does, for people who want to see "what is behind the blocks" or use the Arduino IDE.
// Libraries needed:
//   1. Makeblock (Arduino IDE Library Manager, search "Makeblock", or the copy inside the mBlock 5 install folder)
//   2. MBC_Sensors v2: the four files in src/ of the extension .mext (MBC_Sensors.h/.cpp, mbc_proto.h, mbc_ids.h),
//      put them in Documents/Arduino/libraries/MBC_Sensors/ and #include <MBC_Sensors.h> (https://mbc-pro-sensors.github.io/en/makeblock.html)
// Board: Arduino Uno (the mBot mCore is an Uno). After uploading, unplug USB and run on battery.

#include <MeMCore.h>            // mBot (mCore): motors, LED, buzzer
#include <SoftwareSerial.h>
#include <MBC_Sensors.h>        // MBC sensors v2 (the same library the mBlock extension uses)

MBCPort mbc_port4(4);           // sensor on mBot port 4
MeDCMotor motorL(9);           // left wheel (M1)
MeDCMotor motorR(10);          // right wheel (M2)
MeRGBLed rgbled(7, 2);         // on-board RGB LED (2 pixels)
MeBuzzer buzzer;               // on-board buzzer

// left / right wheel power -100~100 (positive = forward): the mBot left wheel is mounted mirrored, so M1 gets the negative value; % becomes PWM 0~255
void wheels(int l, int r) {
  l = constrain(l, -100, 100); r = constrain(r, -100, 100);
  motorL.run(-l * 255 / 100);
  motorR.run(r * 255 / 100);
}

void setup() {   // everything runs inside setup(), just like the program mBlock generates
  mbc_port4.begin();
  delay(1000);   // Wait 1 s for the receiver to boot
  while (1) {   // Repeat forever
    if ((mbcRead(mbc_port4, 0x06) == 1)) {   // If the gamepad is connected
      rgbled.setColor(0, 0, 255, 0); rgbled.show();   // Connected: green LED
      // Left = left stick y × 0.7, right = right stick y × 0.7
      wheels((mbcReadN(mbc_port4, 0x10, 2, 4) * 0.7), (mbcReadN(mbc_port4, 0x10, 4, 4) * 0.7));
    } else {
      rgbled.setColor(0, 255, 0, 0); rgbled.show();   // Not connected: red LED
      wheels(0, 0);   // Stop
    }
  }
}

void loop() {}   // nothing here: the blocks above never return
```

</details>

**Step by step**
1. Wait 1 s for the receiver to boot
2. Repeat forever
   - If the gamepad is connected
      - Connected: green LED
      - Left = left stick y × 0.7, right = right stick y × 0.7
      - otherwise:
         - Not connected: red LED
         - Stop

**What you should see**: Green LED when the gamepad connects; push both sticks forward and the robot drives, faster the more you push; left forward + right back spins right; switch the gamepad off and it stops at once with a red LED.

**FAQ**
- **Too fast to control?** → Change 0.7 to 0.5.
- **The robot turns the wrong way and gets worse?** → Swap the "+" and "−" (or swap the left and right wheel powers). The mBot ships with the left wheel on M1 and the right on M2; check your own wiring.
- **Buttons and sticks do nothing?** → The gamepad is not connected: run example 5 and check the LED. Red = not connected; power-cycle the gamepad (PS4: press PS), or power the mBot on before plugging in the receiver.
- **Nothing happens, or the value stays at -32768?** → Wrong port (every example on this page uses port 4), socket board not seated, or the sensor is not the Makeblock edition. Check with the "MBC common → connected?" block first; "protocol version" must read 2 for the new firmware (old firmware needs extension v1).
- **Upload fails, or the blocks are blank?** → Make sure the switch at the bottom right is in "Upload" mode, extension v2 has been dropped into mBlock, and the USB cable goes to the mBot board.
